A broker is a person or company whose job is to act as the middleman between two parties — typically a buyer and a seller — and help them complete a deal. The broker brings them together, facilitates the transaction, and earns a fee for doing so.

The single most important thing to understand about a broker: a broker does not own what is being bought or sold. They are a connector, not a trader. Their value is their knowledge, their network of contacts, and their skill in matching the right parties together.

A broker earns a commission — usually a percentage of the total value of the deal. For example, if a broker helps sell a property worth ₹1 crore, they might earn 1% of that (₹1 lakh) as their fee. Sometimes it's a flat fee instead. In most cases, the broker only gets paid when the deal is successfully completed — so they are motivated to make it happen.

Brokers exist in many fields. Here are the most common ones:

Stock broker (Stockbroker)
The stock market is not something you can directly walk into. To buy or sell shares of a company, you need a licensed stockbroker. You tell them what you want, they execute the trade on your behalf on the exchange, and they charge a small fee. Today, many stockbrokers are apps and online platforms, but the role is the same.

Real estate broker
When you want to buy, sell, or rent a property, a real estate broker connects you with the right party. They know the local market, handle negotiations, guide you through legal paperwork, and ensure the deal closes smoothly.

Insurance broker
Instead of approaching one insurance company directly (which is like asking one chef whether their food is the best), an insurance broker approaches multiple insurance companies on your behalf to find you the best coverage at the best price. They work for you, not for the insurer.

Mortgage broker
If you need a home loan, a mortgage broker shops around various banks and lenders to find you the most favourable interest rate and loan terms. They save you the effort of approaching each lender individually.

Commodity broker
These brokers operate in the world of raw materials — gold, crude oil, wheat, cotton, and so on. They connect large buyers and sellers of these commodities and facilitate those trades.

Customs broker
When goods are imported or exported across countries, the paperwork and regulations are complex. A customs broker specialises in handling all the legal formalities, duties, and compliance requirements to move goods smoothly across borders.

Business broker
These brokers help people buy or sell entire businesses. If an entrepreneur wants to sell their company, a business broker finds potential buyers, negotiates the price, and helps close the deal.
How a broker is different from a dealer or merchant

This distinction is important. A dealer or merchant buys the goods themselves and then resells them at a higher price — they take on the risk of ownership. If the goods lose value, that's their loss.

A broker does neither. They never own the asset. They are purely a facilitator. If the deal falls apart, the broker didn't lose any goods — they just lost the commission they would have earned. Their "product" is their service and expertise, not the thing being traded.
A broker's duty to their client

In many countries and industries, a broker is legally required to act in the best interest of their client, not their own. This is known as a fiduciary duty. It means a broker must give you honest advice, find you the best deal available, disclose any conflicts of interest, and not mislead you to earn a bigger commission.

However, not all brokers operate under the same legal standard. Some brokers represent only the buyer, some only the seller, and some try to serve both sides of a transaction. When working with a broker, it is always wise to ask clearly: "Whose interests are you representing?"

The word broker is also used figuratively to describe someone who wields significant behind-the-scenes influence. A power broker is someone whose connections and leverage allow them to make important things happen, negotiate agreements between powerful parties, and shape outcomes without necessarily being in a formal position of authority. A senior political figure who quietly negotiates between rival factions to form a government coalition, for instance, would be called a power broker.

Similarly, when you hear "she brokered a peace deal between the two warring sides," it means she acted as the intermediary who brought those sides together and helped them reach an agreement.

A broker is an intermediary — someone who connects two parties, most commonly a buyer and a seller, to help them complete a transaction. They do not own the goods or assets involved. They earn their income through a commission or fee paid upon the successful completion of a deal. Their worth comes from their expertise, industry knowledge, and relationships. Brokers exist in virtually every field where complex transactions happen: financial markets, real estate, insurance, loans, commodities, international trade, and more. Whether in a formal professional sense or in everyday figurative language, the word always carries the same essential idea: someone who stands in the middle and makes things happen between two parties.
